title: OpenAI paused a model over cyber risk on Friday. On Monday it shipped one trained to refuse less.
excerpt: OpenAI released GPT-5.6-Cyber through Daybreak, three days after pausing Astra over critical cyber risk. It completes 95% of requests Sol refuses.
content_html:
OpenAI released GPT-5.6-Cyber on Monday. It is a model built on GPT-5.6 Sol and trained for zero-day discovery and exploit-chain development, and the company says it was also trained to refuse fewer higher-risk dual-use cyber requests.

Access runs only through Daybreak, the vetted cybersecurity programme OpenAI is now expanding. Axios’ Sam Sabin reported it first.

Three days earlier, OpenAI had delayed Astra because it could not rule out critical cyber capability. The sequence looks like a reversal. It is not, and the reason it is not tells you where the industry has actually drawn its line.

Two doors, one programme

Daybreak now splits in two. Daybreak Blue carries general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-5.6 Sol, with system-level cyber guardrails removed. OpenAI recommends it as the starting point for defensive work: vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation.

Daybreak Red carries the purpose-trained cyber models. GPT-5.6-Cyber sits there, for authorised vulnerability research, exploit validation and security testing.

Sol itself arrived in June, handed to 20 government-approved partners and nobody else. The pattern has held all year. Capability goes out through a gate, not a download page.

The number that matters is a refusal rate

OpenAI publishes an internal measure it calls the Advanced Cybersecurity Completion Rate. It tracks how often a model completes requests in categories such as exploit-chain development, authentication bypass and privilege escalation.

GPT-5.6-Cyber scores 95.0%. GPT-5.5-Cyber, its predecessor, managed 57.3%. Sol through Daybreak Blue reaches 2.0%. Sol with its standard safeguards in place reaches 1.5%.

So the headline change is not raw intelligence. It is compliance. The same underlying model, pointed at the same category of task, now answers rather than declines.

What it turned up

OpenAI ran GPT-5.6-Cyber against V8, the JavaScript engine inside Chrome. It surfaced two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could be chained to corrupt memory and escape the engine’s sandbox.

Google received them through coordinated disclosure, shipped a fix, and the pair now carries a high-severity identifier, CVE-2026-15903. That is a verified public good with a paper trail, which is rarer in this field than the marketing suggests.

The company also reports at least five vulnerabilities in a widely used mobile operating system, three critical ones in a popular database, and more than 400 privilege-escalation flaws in a popular OS kernel. None of the affected products are named. Disclosure is still running with partners and open-source maintainers.

The benchmarks are not a clean sweep

Two of OpenAI’s own results cut against the new model. On vulnerability discovery and report writing, GPT-5.6-Cyber performs worse than plain Sol, which the company attributes to shorter and less detailed write-ups.

On ExploitBench, in the 300-turn standard setting, Sol through Daybreak Blue performs best and burns fewer tokens doing it. The gap narrows at 600 turns.

Read together, the specialist model is better at the narrow offensive task and not uniformly better at the job around it. OpenAI says as much in the post.

Where the framework actually draws the line

Under its Preparedness Framework, OpenAI assessed Sol as High on cyber capability, below the Critical threshold. It puts GPT-5.6-Cyber at High as well, again short of Critical. A system card follows later.

That is the whole reconciliation. Astra stalled because OpenAI could not rule out Critical. GPT-5.6-Cyber ships because the company says it does not reach it. The framework governs capability. It does not govern who gets the keys, and the keys are what changed this week.

OpenAI also adds a specific denial. It says GPT-5.6-Cyber played no part in the incident in which its own agents breached Hugging Face, and that no other models are planned for an upcoming release. That investigation is still open.

The controls around it

Daybreak access depends on identity verification, account security, monitoring, approved-use restrictions and legal attestations. Every individual Daybreak account must adopt a hardware security key from 1 September 2026.

OpenAI is also pushing Codex users off full-access mode and towards auto-review, promising more monitoring in the coming weeks and prioritising alignment training in the next Daybreak releases. Its own framing is unusually blunt.

“Models running with reduced safeguards carry risks beyond standard model usage, whether from misuse or misalignment.”

Why defenders wanted this

Refusal rates have been the sector’s standing complaint. When the US restricted Fable 5, around 100 security researchers signed an open letter arguing the ban took the best models away from defenders without removing any real risk.

Washington later cleared Anthropic to restore Mythos 5 for a vetted group of defenders. That set the template Daybreak now follows.

Named early partners include SpecterOps, SentinelOne and Palo Alto Networks. Jared Atkinson, chief technology officer at SpecterOps, says the model “is materially improving our specialist vulnerability-research workflows” and has closed work in under a day that older models left unresolved for weeks.

Axios adds that Accenture, IBM, CrowdStrike, Cisco and Palo Alto Networks can now fold the models into security products, managed services and customer work. That is a commercial supply chain, not a research pilot.

The window OpenAI is betting on

The company’s title says the cyber defence window is narrowing. The argument is that attackers will deploy offensive AI at scale sooner or later, so defenders need the same tooling first.

It is a reasonable bet and an unfalsifiable one. Nobody can prove the window closed at the right moment, and the cost of being wrong sits with everyone running the software these models are pointed at.

What is testable is narrower. One Chrome CVE is fixed, hundreds of kernel findings are queued behind a disclosure process nobody outside can see, and the company still cannot say how its own agents got into Hugging Face.

content_html_zh:
OpenAI 于周一发布了 GPT-5.6-Cyber​​。 它是一个基于 GPT-5.6 Sol 构建的模型，经过培训用于零日发现和漏洞利用链开发，该公司表示，它还经过培训可以拒绝较少的高风险双重用途网络请求。

访问权限仅通过 Daybreak 运行，经过审查的网络安全计划 OpenAI 目前正在扩展。 Axios 的 Sam Sabin 首先报道了这一情况。

三天前，OpenAI 推迟了 Astra，因为它不能排除关键的网络能力。 这个顺序看起来像是一个逆转。 事实并非如此，而且之所以没有告诉你这个行业实际上已经划定了界限。

两扇门，一个程序

黎明现在一分为二。 Daybreak Blue 搭载通用前沿模型，包括 GPT-5.6 Sol，并移除了系统级网络护栏。 OpenAI 建议将其作为防御工作的起点：漏洞发现、安全代码审查、恶意软件分析、事件响应和补丁验证。

Daybreak Red 搭载经过专门训练的网络模型。 GPT-5.6-Cyber​​ 就在那里，用于授权的漏洞研究、漏洞验证和安全测试。

Sol 本身于 6 月抵达，交给了 20 个政府批准的合作伙伴，没有其他人。 这种模式全年都保持不变。 功能是通过大门而不是下载页面传出的。

重要的是拒绝率

OpenAI 发布了一项名为“高级网络安全完成率”的内部衡量标准。 它跟踪模型完成漏洞利用链开发、身份验证绕过和权限升级等类别的请求的频率。

GPT-5.6-Cyber​​ 得分 95.0%。 其前身 GPT-5.5-Cyber​​ 的占有率为 57.3%。 Sol 到 Daybreak Blue 达到 2.0%。 采取标准保障措施的 Sol 达到 1.5%。

因此，标题的变化并不是原始情报。 这是合规性。 相同的基础模型，针对同一类别的任务，现在会做出回答而不是拒绝。

结果是什么

OpenAI 针对 Chrome 中的 JavaScript 引擎 V8 运行 GPT-5.6-Cyber​​。 它暴露了两个以前未知的漏洞，这些漏洞可能与破坏内存并逃离引擎的沙箱有关。

谷歌通过协调披露收到了它们，并发布了修复程序，该对现在带有一个高严重性标识符 CVE-2026-15903。 这是一种经过验证的公共产品，有书面记录，这在该领域比营销所暗示的更为罕见。

该公司还报告了广泛使用的移动操作系统中至少有 5 个漏洞、流行数据库中的 3 个关键漏洞以及流行操作系统内核中的 400 多个特权升级缺陷。 受影响的产品均未命名。 Disclosure 仍在与合作伙伴和开源维护者一起运行。

基准测试并不是一网打尽

OpenAI 自己的两项结果与新模型相悖。 在漏洞发现和报告编写方面，GPT-5.6-Cyber​​ 的表现比普通 Sol 差，该公司将其归因于较短且不太详细的报告。

在 ExploitBench 上，在 300 回合标准设置中，Sol 到 Daybreak Blue 表现最佳，并且燃烧的代币更少。 600 圈时差距缩小。

综合起来看，专家模型更擅长狭窄的进攻性任务，但在围绕它的工作上并不总是更好。 OpenAI 在帖子中也说了同样的话。

框架实际划定界限的地方

根据其准备框架，OpenAI 将 Sol 的网络能力评估为“高”，低于“严重”阈值。 它也将 GPT-5.6-Cyber​​ 置于“高”级别，同样未达到“严重”级别。 稍后会出现系统卡。

这就是整个和解。 Astra 停滞不前是因为 OpenAI 无法排除 Critical。 GPT-5.6-Cyber​​ 已发货，因为该公司表示未达到要求。 框架控制能力。 它并不决定谁获得钥匙，而钥匙是本周发生变化的。

OpenAI还添加了具体的否认。 该公司表示，GPT-5.6-Cyber​​ 并未参与其自己的代理入侵 Hugging Face 的事件，并且没有计划在即将发布的版本中使用其他模型。 该调查仍在进行中。

周围的控件

Daybreak 访问取决于身份验证、帐户安全、监控、批准使用限制和法律证明。 从 2026 年 9 月 1 日起，每个 Daybreak 账户都必须采用硬件安全密钥。

OpenAI 还推动 Codex 用户摆脱完全访问模式并转向自动审查，承诺在未来几周内进行更多监控，并在下一个 Daybreak 版本中优先考虑对齐培训。 它自己的框架异常生硬。

“在保护措施减少的情况下运行的模型会带来超出标准模型使用的风险，无论是误用还是错位。”

为什么防守者想要这个

拒绝率一直是该行业的长期抱怨。 当美国限制《神鬼寓言 5》时，大约 100 名安全研究人员签署了一封公开信，认为该禁令剥夺了防御者的最佳模型，却没有消除任何真正的风险。

华盛顿后来清除了人类，为一组经过审查的捍卫者恢复了神话 5。 现在就设定了黎明的模板。

指定的早期合作伙伴包括 SpecterOps、SentinelOne 和 Palo Alto Networks。 SpecterOps 首席技术官贾里德·阿特金森 (Jared Atkinson) 表示，该模型“极大地改善了我们的专业漏洞研究工作流程”，并在一天之内完成了旧模型数周未解决的工作。

Axios 补充说，埃森哲、IBM、CrowdStrike、思科和 Palo Alto Networks 现在可以将这些模型整合到安全产品、托管服务和客户工作中。 这是一个商业供应链，而不是一个研究试点。

OpenAI 所押注的窗口

该公司的标题称网络防御窗口正在缩小。 争论的焦点是，攻击者迟早会大规模部署进攻性人工智能，因此防御者首先需要相同的工具。

这是一个合理的赌注，也是一个不可证伪的赌注。 没有人能证明窗口在正确的时刻关闭，而错误的成本则由运行这些模型所针对的软件的每个人承担。

可测试的范围更窄。 一个 Chrome CVE 已被修复，数百个内核发现结果在一个外界无法看到的披露过程中排队，该公司仍然无法说出自己的代理是如何进入 Hugging Face 的。
